paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Many scientists believe that socialisation is a long process, while compliance is its starting point. Promoting compliance in children is therefore a priority. Motivationally distinct forms of child compliance, mutually positive affect, and maternal control, observed in three control contexts in 103 dyads of mothers and their 26- to 41-month-old children, were examined as correlates of internalization, assessed using observations of children while alone with prohibited temptations and maternal ratings. One form of compliance (committed compliance), when the child appeared committed wholeheartedly to the maternal agenda and eager to endorse and accept it, was emphasized. Mother-child mutually positive affect was both a predictor and a concomitant of committed compliance. Children who shared positive affect with their mothers showed a high level of committed compliance and were also more internalized. Differences and similarities between children’s compliance with requests and prohibitions (“Do” vs. “Don’t” demand contexts) were also explored. Maternal “Dos” appeared more challenging to toddlers than the “Don’ts.” Some individual coherence of behavior was also found across both demand contexts. The implication of committed compliance for emerging internalized regulators of conduct is discussed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some parents found it difficult to recognise compliance, and some even overlooked their children’s noncompliance. Despite receiving a good education, children did not always obey their parents, especially boys at certain ages. This level of noncompliance was considered acceptable, and some parents responded patiently. Some researchers argued that noncompliance is not necessarily wrong. To determine the effects of different parental disciplinary techniques on young children’s compliance and noncompliance, mothers were trained to observe emotional incidents involving their toddler-aged children. Reports of disciplinary encounters were analysed in terms of the types of discipline used (reasoning, verbal prohibition, physical coercion, love withdrawal, and combinations thereof) and children’s responses (compliance, noncompliance and avoidance). The relationship between compliance or noncompliance and the type of misdeed (harm to people, harm to property, and lapses of self-control) was also analysed. Results indicated that love withdrawal combined with other techniques was most effective in securing children’s compliance, regardless of the technique with which it was combined. Avoidant responses and emotional reunification with the parent were more likely to follow love withdrawal than any other technique. Physical coercion was somewhat less effective, while reasoning and verbal prohibition were ineffective unless both were combined with physical coercion.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: “When children are younger, they sometimes express noncompliance directly, but as they grow older they may learn more sophisticated approaches. They become more skilful at negotiating or giving reasons for refusing, rather than directly opposing their parents,” said Henry Porter, a scholar at a psychology institute in the UK. He suggested that noncompliance can reflect development and may benefit children in some ways. Many experts have held different views in recent years, and some have tried to instil compliance in children. Porter’s collaborator, Wallace Friesen, argued that a child’s daily activities should occur in the same order each day as much as possible. This first strategy for defiant children is ultimately the most important. Developing a routine helps a child know what to expect and increases the chances that he or she will comply with chores, homework and hygiene requests. When undesirable activities occur in the same order at suitable times during the day, they become habits that are carried out without question. You have probably developed routines for showering, cleaning your house or doing other types of work. You know when you will do these things regularly, and this helps you know what to expect. In fact, you have probably already been using most of these compliance strategies yourself without realising it. Children can become very upset if daily expectations are not made part of a regular routine. Like adults, children think about what they plan to do each day and expect to be able to do what they want. When you ask them to do something they had not planned, the result can be automatic refusal or other defiant behaviour. Using this compliance strategy with defiant children ensures that activities are completed almost every day in the same general order, so the child expects to do them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dr Steven Walson argued that enjoyable activities should follow activities that children frequently resist. This strategy also works as positive reinforcement when the child complies with a request. Arranging the day so that frequently resisted activities occur immediately before highly preferred ones can reduce defiant behaviour and motivate the child to perform the undesirable activity. This should not be presented as though the preferred activity is allowed only if the child completes the non-preferred one. Instead, word the request so that the child understands that the non-preferred activity must be completed before moving on to the preferred activity. For example, do not say, “If you clean your room, we can play a game.” Instead, say, “As soon as you have finished cleaning your room, we can play that really fun game you wanted to play.”

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Psychologist Paul Edith insisted that praise is the best way to encourage children to comply. This is probably familiar advice: if you praise a child’s behaviour, he or she is more likely to repeat it. Praise is therefore essential when working with defiant children, and it also gives the child positive attention. However, praise must be delivered in a way that encourages the child to repeat the behaviour without prompting.

Questions 27–31
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
Write your answers in boxes 27–31 on your answer sheet.
27 Children—especially boys—who receive a good education may
 A always obey their parents.
 B be good at mathematics.
 C achieve high scores at school.
 D sometimes disobey their parents’ instructions.

28 When dealing with their children’s compliance and noncompliance, parents
 A must recognise compliant behaviour.
 B should ask teachers for help.
 C may overlook noncompliant behaviour.
 D may pretend not to notice it.

29 According to Henry Porter, noncompliance in children
 A is entirely harmful.
 B may have positive effects.
 C requires medical assistance.
 D should be treated by a specialist.

30 When children are growing up, they
 A always refuse directly.
 B become more skilful at negotiating.
 C learn to deceive rather than disobey.
 D tend to keep silent

31 Which response to parental instructions is associated with older or younger children in the
passage?
 A Older children prefer to refuse directly.
 B Older children refuse to answer.
 C Younger children may refuse directly.
 D Younger children may remain silent.
